notes:
I've put together notes on all 23 verses of Jeremiah 18 below. I found good material from the older commentaries and from Reformed, Wesleyan, Lutheran and Churches of Christ writers. I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites, or on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so those are left out. Some verses (5, 16 and 19) have only thin notes.

Two things to know about labels and links. The tradition tags are my own, not taken from the pages: Matthew Henry and Calvin as Reformed, Gill as Baptist, Adam Clarke as Methodist, Keil & Delitzsch as Lutheran, Ellicott as Anglican, Coffman as Churches of Christ. The citation brackets only work for pages that came up in search results. Notes from two pages I opened directly are just followed by the link: Utley at bible.org and the NET Bible notes.

---

## Jeremiah 18: verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Coffman says the chapter comes early in Jehoiakim's reign, while repentance was still possible. Chapter 19's broken jar then shows the kingdom's final overthrow. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik says God sometimes taught His prophets through a living lesson, something from daily life. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- Barnes places the potters' clay-field…to the south of Jerusalem just beyond the valley of Hinnom. Ellicott links it to the "potter's field" of Zechariah 11:13. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/18-2.htm and https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/18-2.htm
- Coffman ties this field to Matthew 27, where Judas's thirty pieces of silver bought a burial plot. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html
- Matthew Henry notes that Jeremiah was sent to receive a sermon ready prepared, not to preach one. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_018.cfm

**v. 3**
- Gill says the word means the thing the potter worked on, not his seat. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) translates it "on stones."  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/18-3.htm
- Coffman, quoting Ash, describes two stone wheels on one shaft. The lower, heavier wheel was turned by foot and the upper one shaped the pot. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html

**v. 4**
- Utley says the problem was defective clay, not an unskilled potter. The clay is fallen, as in Genesis 3. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18
- Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: the potter did not abandon it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- The Biblical Illustrator says human clay has the power of resistance. The lesson is to cooperate rather than resist. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/jeremiah-18.html

**v. 5**
- The NET notes say verses 7–10 are spoken to Jeremiah himself. Verse 6 is a sudden turn to address Israel directly (the figure of speech called "apostrophe"). — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Jer+18:7-10

**v. 6**
- **Matthew Henry:** God has an incontestable sovereignty over us, is not debtor to us. If people are not glorified by Him, He will be glorified upon them, citing Proverbs 16:4. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_018.cfm
- **Adam Clarke:** God has the right to act as reason and justice may require. He limits the image to destinies here below, and reads the related Romans 9 picture as being about honourable and humbler callings. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-18.html
- **Guzik:** like any analogy, this one does not fit at every point. the clay has no moral choice or dimension, whereas Israel's disobedience was chosen again and again. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- **Joseph Parker:** The potter did not reason with the clay: God did reason with Israel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/jeremiah-18.html
- Coffman, following Paul in Romans 9:21, says the marred clay (Israel) became a "vessel unto dishonor." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html

**vv. 7–10 (God "relents")** *This is where traditions differ most.*
- **NET (modern scholarship):** translators debate the word. Some avoid "change my mind" because of Numbers 23:19, but "relent" may not convey the actual change of course in view. NET suggests "revoke" or "forgo." It also notes a wordplay: "evil" means both the crime and the punishment, as in Jonah 3–4. — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Jer+18:7-10
- The five verbs (uproot, tear down, destroy, build, plant) echo Jeremiah's call in 1:10.  — same URL
- **Matthew Henry (Reformed):** God though he cannot change his mind, he will change his way. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_018.cfm
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel), quoting Feinberg:** for God, "repentance" is not a change of mind but His consistent response to a change in the nation's conduct. The main lesson is that God is free to respond to moral choices.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- **Reformed response to open theism (The Gospel Coalition):**
  - D. A. Carson explains that open theists favour this passage. For them the potter image is "not deterministic."  — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/part-2-portrait-of-a-limited-god/
  - Another TGC sermon answers that God is not talking here about his eternal decree but about His "providential declaration of intent," which can be adjusted. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/interpretation-part-1/
- **Coffman (Churches of Christ):** all of God's promises and threats are absolutely and eternally conditional. He says this passage refutes "faith only," "once saved, always saved," and the idea that the land belongs to the Jewish people forever. This sharply opposes the Baptist and Reformed doctrine of perseverance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html
- **BibleHub (evangelical):** God does not literally discover new information, and "reconsideration" reflects the human view of events in time. — https://biblehub.com/q/how_can_god_'reconsider'_if_unchanging.htm
- **Utley (evangelical):** this is where the doctrine of "God's Sovereignty" and "Human Freewill" meet! — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18

**v. 11**
- Harrison, quoted by Guzik: "fashioning" disaster uses the same root as "potter," and The nation is to be moulded by means of the Exile. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- Guzik says the lesson rebuked Judah's false confidence that, as God's covenant people, no harm could come to them.  — same URL
- Utley notes that true repentance is turning to good, not only turning from evil. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18

**v. 12**
- NET says the verb form (a vav-consecutive perfect) points to the future: Judah's response is predictable. — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Jer+18:7-10
- Guzik: "hopeless" means it's not worth changing their evil hearts just because one prophet told them to. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- Matthew Henry: people call it liberty to live as they please, but for a man to be a slave to his lusts is the worst of slaveries. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_018.cfm

**v. 13**
- Coffman says Israel's forsaking of its God had no parallel among ancient peoples, and calling her "virgin" heightens the horror. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html
- Utley explains "a most terrible thing" as a nation changing its god. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18

**v. 14** (a hard verse to translate)
- Ellicott says the AV's added words "a man" distort the verse. The questions expect a "no" and restate Jeremiah 2:13 poetically.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/18-14.htm
- Poole lists the differing ancient versions but says the general sense is clear: it is foolish to forsake God.  — same URL
- The Cambridge Bible accepts a small change to the Hebrew letters ("dried up") and the reading "Sirion" (another name for Mount Hermon). — same URL
- Calvin sees a twofold madness in rejecting kindness close at hand. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/18-14.html
- Utley: nature behaves predictably, but not the seed of Abraham! — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18

**v. 15**
- Coffman, quoting a source: the "ancient ways" are covenant loyalty, the "good way" of 6:16. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html
- Utley lists Isaiah's "highway" theme as background. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18

**v. 16**
- Utley: the people meant to be a light to the nations became an object of scorn. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18

**v. 17**
- Utley: "My back and not My face" depends on re-pointing the vowels of the standard Hebrew text. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18
- Coffman: God withdraws His favour just as the people had turned their backs on Him (2:27). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html

**v. 18**
- Utley: this is the only Old Testament verse naming all three channels of revelation together: priest (law), sage (counsel) and prophet (word). The Septuagint reads "listen to find fault." — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18
- Guzik: the leaders assumed that holding a title meant having God's word. Quoting Thompson, he says these establishment men probably led the plot.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- Coffman, quoting Payne Smith: they assumed the Law's guardians could not perish, so they treated Jeremiah's message as blasphemy. Coffman sees a parallel with the charges against Christ. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html

**vv. 19–20**
- Utley: "dug a pit" is a hunting image. It may mean a real plan to kill him, or ruining his reputation. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18
- Guzik: Jeremiah had prayed good for the very people who were now trying to kill him.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/

**vv. 21–23 (the curse prayer)** *Traditions differ here too.*
- **Guzik:** like the imprecatory psalms, the prayer hands vengeance over to God instead of taking it.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
- **Utley:** the requests are "hyperbolic prophetic imperatives" (deliberate exaggeration). Jeremiah was troubled more by Judah's sin than by his own suffering. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-18
- **Calvin (Reformed):** the prayer was limited to the reprobate and irreclaimable. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/18-23.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** they had committed something like the unpardonable sin or "sin unto death" (1 John 5:16). — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/jeremiah/18-23.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Jeremiah prayed by prophetic impulse. Copying him, we know not what manner of spirit we are of. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/18-23.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** they reject Calvin's view and say that since Christ, Old Testament retribution cannot be for us the standard. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/18-23.htm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** For us such prayers are among the things that have passed away. Barnes (Presbyterian) says they belong to the legal spirit of the Jewish covenant. — same URL
- **Coffman (Churches of Christ):** pushes back against the critics. He likens the prayer to the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:10. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-18.html
- **Poole:** "not forgiving" may mean punishment in this life, not damnation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/18-23.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "overthrown" literally means "made to stumble." — same URL
- **Thompson, via Guzik and Coffman:** God gives no recorded answer to this prayer. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-18/
